idiom_name: Rails.cache.fetch around the full-page render, with stale? for conditional GETs
implementation_notes: Rails supplies the building blocks rather than one switch: Rails.cache.fetch(key, expires_in:) computes the page on a miss and stores the finished HTML in the configured store (Solid Cache, Redis, memcached, filesystem), so hits skip the view and the queries behind it, while stale?(last_modified:, etag:) answers If-None-Match/If-Modified-Since with a 304 for clients that already hold a copy - Rails' guide documents this conditional-GET support directly. Invalidation is key-based (bump cache_key_with_version, touch the models the page depends on, or delete the key explicitly), and the store-backed form is the one that works across several servers, which is why the file/disk variant survives mainly for the purely anonymous case.
code_sketch:
def show
  html = Rails.cache.fetch(["article", params[:slug], I18n.locale],
                           expires_in: 5.minutes) do
    render_to_string(:article)          # controller, queries and views on a miss only
  end
  if stale?(last_modified: @article.updated_at.utc, etag: @article.cache_key)
    response.set_header("Cache-Control", "public, max-age=300")
    render html: html
  end
end
pitfalls: A shared store means a key that omits locale, currency or user serves one variant to everyone - put every varying axis into the key array.
render_to_string inside the cache block freezes controller state into the entry: whatever the template reads outside the key (current_user, flash, request) is baked into the cached HTML.
expires_in is a freshness hint, not a purge: publishing still needs an explicit cache delete (or touch) or the site shows the old page until the TTL lapses.

Action Pack page caching (caches_page, static files under public/)
variants.idiom_name: caches_page / expire_page from the actionpack-page_caching gem
variants.implementation_notes: The original and purest form in Rails: caches_page :show makes Action Pack write the finished response body to a file whose path mirrors the URL (public/posts/what-is-new.html), and the web server serves that file directly, so a cache hit never reaches Rails at all; config.action_controller.page_cache_directory moves the tree, expire_page (or a sweeper/observer on model changes) deletes entries. It was removed from core in Rails 4.0 and lives on as the actionpack-page_caching gem, whose README states the restriction plainly: only GET/HEAD responses with status 200 are cached, the technique suits content sites (wikis, documentation) and not account-based systems. Choose it when pages are anonymous and the web server is already the fastest place to serve files, and remember the cache directory is per server unless it is shared.
variants.code_sketch:
class ArticlesController < ApplicationController
  caches_page :show                     # writes public/articles/<slug>.html

  def update
    Article.update(params[:id], params[:article])
    expire_page action: "show", id: params[:id]   # delete the stale file
    redirect_to action: "show", id: params[:id]
  end
end
pitfalls: Files are never expired automatically: without expire_page (or a directory-level purge) the site keeps serving the old HTML indefinitely.
page_cache_directory must be writable by the app and readable by the web server, and a directory shared across servers needs a distributed filesystem - which usually defeats the point.
Cached files bypass the Rails stack entirely, so authentication, instrumentation and logging do not run for hits; only genuinely public pages may be cached this way.
